content:
Most AI startups are features wearing a startup costume. If your entire product calls a third-party model API with a cleaner interface on top, you are one product release away from irrelevance. The question worth asking before you hire your first engineer: what do you own that nobody can replicate by simply switching API providers?

Key Takeaways

  • 78% of AI startups launched in 2024 were thin API wrappers; about 65% churned early users within 90 days
  • OpenAI ships native features roughly every six weeks, each capable of making a product category redundant overnight
  • Indian AI startup funding hit $1.48 billion in Q1 2026, but nearly all went to companies with enterprise revenue already in hand
  • Proprietary data and deep workflow lock-in are the moats that hold up; distribution incumbents cannot reach is a powerful third
  • Indian-language AI infrastructure and sovereign compute are among the hardest moats to copy today

What Is Actually Happening to AI Startups Right Now

Indian AI startups raised $1.48 billion in Q1 2026, roughly six times all of 2025 combined. That sounds generous. It isn't, for most founders. Seed-stage funding fell 30% in the same quarter. The startups raising big rounds shared one trait: enterprise revenue before the raise. Not projected. Actual.

78% of AI startups launched in 2024 were thin API wrappers. About 65% had churned their initial users within 90 days. The survivors weren't the ones with the cleverest prompts. They owned something their users couldn't get by pasting a question directly into ChatGPT.

What Sherlocking Does to Your Business

Sherlocking is what happens when OpenAI or Google ships a native feature that makes your standalone product redundant. Since 2024, this has happened to PDF summarizers, writing assistants, code explanation tools, and general-purpose chatbots. At least 200 funded startups became unnecessary overnight. Google Cloud's VP of AI partnerships said in February 2026 that startups wrapping thin IP around Gemini or GPT-5 face extinction.

Many of these products were genuinely useful. The problem is that "useful but not defensable" is an expensive place to build a business. Users don't feel guilty switching to the native version. They barely remember the product's name.

Three Questions That Tell You Where You Stand

Three questions cut through the pitch deck. Answer them honestly before you raise.

One: Can a user get the same result by pasting your system prompt into Claude and uploading the same file? If the honest answer is "our UI is nicer," you have a feature.

Two: If OpenAI ships this capability natively next quarter, does your company still exist? A "no" means you're one press release away from a bad investor call.

Three: What do you own that gets more valuable the longer customers stay? Proprietary data gets richer. Deep workflow integrations create real switching costs. A trusted distribution channel, like a network of 40,000 chartered accountants in India, compounds over time. Many founders treat these as seperate questions when they're really asking just one: what are you building that can't be copied?

What Is Actually Working in India

Two types of Indian AI startups are getting funded at real multiples right now.

The first builds infrastructure. Krutrim built a 12-billion parameter multilingual model and its own GPU cloud before raising at scale. Sarvam built model infrastructure optimised for India's 22 official languages and reached a $1.5 billion valuation because production-quality support for Kannada or Marathi is genuinely hard to replicate. The moat is years deep.

The second type owns a specific workflow. Harvey, the legal AI company, integrates with how law firms bill, review, and file. Switching away from it costs real money. Rocketlane doubled revenue before closing its Series C because it owned a process its customers couldn't easily abandon. This pattern holds accross categories where the highest-value data is generated inside the workflow itself.

Neither started with the best AI. Both started by knowing exactly who their user is, what that user does instead today, and what it would actually cost to switch back.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is an AI wrapper startup?

An AI wrapper calls a foundation model's API, usually GPT, Claude, or Gemini, and presents the output inside a custom interface. No model training happens. The value comes from the prompt, the UI, or the workflow. About 78% of AI startups launched in 2024 were wrappers, and most have since stagnated or shut down.

Can a wrapper startup succeed?

Yes, if a real moat sits on top of the API. Cursor is technically a wrapper around code models but became the default IDE for many developers through deep workflow integration. Harvey generates over $100 million in annual revenue as a legal AI wrapper. The wrapper alone is not enough. The moat is what matters.

How much are Indian AI startups raising in 2026?

Indian AI startups raised $1.48 billion in Q1 2026 alone, six times the full-year 2025 total. H1 2026 crossed $1 billion. But seed-stage funding fell 30%. Rounds go to startups with real enterprise traction. Founders pitching AI potential without demonstrable revenue are finding it significantly harder to close deals.

What is the sherlocking risk for AI startups?

Sherlocking happens when a model provider ships a native feature that replaces a standalone product. OpenAI has done this to hundreds of funded startups since 2024, across PDF tools, writing assistants, and support bots. Any product whose core value comes only from prompt engineering over a public API faces this risk on the next release cycle.

What moats actually hold up for Indian AI startups?

Two moats hold up consistently: proprietary data from transactions, filings, or healthcare records that improve the model over time; and deep workflow integration that makes switching genuinely painful. Supporting India's 22 official languages at production quality is a third that's especially hard to copy. Distribution through trusted channels, like cooperative banks, also compounds over time.

The Short Version

A real AI business owns something that compounds: data that gets richer, a workflow that gets stickier, or a distribution channel incumbents can't replicate. If you pull out the AI layer and the business collapses into a blank page, that is not your moat. That is your vendor.
